docs.title: Manage Your Claude.ai Memory
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A practical guide to viewing, editing, and controlling what Claude remembers about you.

docs.title: What Is Claude's Memory?
docs.text:
Claude.ai has two memory mechanisms:

  • Auto-generated memory — Claude analyzes your conversation history roughly every 24 hours and synthesizes key context (your job, preferences, projects, etc.) into a memory profile.
  • User-directed edits — Things you explicitly tell Claude to remember or forget. These are stored as discrete entries (up to 30 slots, ~100 characters each).

Note: Memory is scoped separately for regular chats vs. Projects. Information from inside a Project only applies to that Project.

docs.title: Enabling Memory
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Capabilities
  2. Toggle on "Generate memory from chat history"
  3. This is the core switch — Claude won't build a memory profile without it.
  4. Optionally enable "Search and reference chats"
  5. This allows Claude to search back through past conversations for relevant details. Useful, but not required for basic memory.

docs.title: Viewing Your Memory
docs.text:
Once Claude has accumulated enough context:

  1. Go to Settings → Capabilities
  2. Click "View and edit memory" in the Memory section
  3. The Manage Memory modal shows everything Claude currently remembers about you

You can also ask Claude directly in any chat:

What do you remember about me?

docs.title: Adding to Memory
docs.text:
Option A — Tell Claude in chat: 

Please remember that I work as a Python programmer.
Remember that I prefer dark mode in all tools.

Option B — Via the memory modal: 1. Open Settings → Capabilities → View and edit memory 2. Click the pencil icon in the lower-left corner of the summary 3. Type the information you want added

Any edits made this way apply immediately to your next conversation.

docs.title: Editing Existing Memory
docs.text:
To update a specific fact: 

Update your memory — I no longer work at Acme Corp, I now work at Example Inc.

To correct something: 

You have my job title wrong. I'm a senior engineer, not a junior engineer.

Claude will use the memory tool to update the entry in place.

docs.title: Deleting / Forgetting Memory
docs.text:
To remove a specific item: 

Please forget that I mentioned my old company.
Forget about my preference for tabs over spaces.

To clear everything: 1. Go to Settings → Capabilities 2. Click "Reset memory" 3. Confirm

Warning: Resetting memory permanently deletes all memories and cannot be undone.

docs.title: Pausing Memory (Without Deleting)
docs.text:
If you want Claude to stop learning new things without wiping existing memory:

  1. Go to Settings → Capabilities
  2. Select "Pause memory"

Claude will retain its current memory but won't add new entries or reference it until you re-enable it.

docs.title: Using Incognito Mode
docs.text:
For conversations you don't want to influence your memory profile at all:

  • Click the ghost icon in the top-right corner of a new chat to enable Incognito mode
  • Incognito chats are never added to memory, regardless of your settings

docs.title: Tips for Getting the Most Out of Memory
docs.text: Do Avoid Reserve explicit edits for stable, permanent facts Burning edit slots on temporary context Use Project knowledge bases for project-specific info Relying on memory across different Projects Periodically review and prune outdated entries Letting old/irrelevant facts accumulate Use Incognito for sensitive or one-off conversations Sharing sensitive info in regular chats

  2. Click "Start Import" under Import memory from other AI providers
  3. Claude will generate a prompt you can use to export your context from the other service, then import it

docs.title: Understand Cowork and Dispatch
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Claude can operate apps on your computer (browser, spreadsheets, email) to complete tasks while you focus on other things.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Dispatch — Assign tasks from your phone; Claude runs them on your desktop
  • Scheduled tasks — Set recurring tasks (e.g. daily inbox scan, weekly reports)
  • Persistent context — Claude remembers previous work so tasks pick up where they left off
  • No configuration needed — Claude uses connected apps first, then browser or screen

docs.title: How to Get Started
docs.text:
1. Leave your desktop awake
  2. Open Dispatch in Claude Desktop
  3. Pair with the mobile app
  4. Hand off your first task from anywhere

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• These are research previews — complex tasks may need more than one attempt
  • Available on Pro and Max plans only
  • Computer use is limited to macOS — Windows users can use Dispatch but cannot use the full computer control feature yet

Note: Windows users can use Dispatch, but the "Claude operates your screen" feature is not yet available. No release date has been announced.

docs.title: Add a MyCoeiroInk Voice to CoeiroInk
Add a MyCoeiroInk Voice to CoeiroInk
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

MyCoeiroInk is the community voice library for CoeiroInk, where creators distribute downloadable voice characters.

Example voice used: 白痴ー (Hakuchi) One of the most popular male voices on MyCoeiroInk, available in multiple style variations. The voice can also be used as a character called 黒聡 鵜月 (Kurosato Uzuki).

docs.title: Step 1: Download the Voice
docs.text:
1. Go to https://coeiroink.com/mycoeiroink.
  2. Click the center illustration 探す (Sagasu / Search), which navigates to the voice list at https://coeiroink.com/mycoeiroink/list.
  3. Enter 白痴ー (Hakuchi) in the search box and press Enter.
  4. Click the 白痴ー panel in the results — this navigates to the distribution page on BOOTH.
  5. Choose and download a variation as a ZIP file.

Note: 白痴ー (Hakuchi) is distributed as multiple separate ZIP files, each representing a different style:

File name Romaji Style 若輩.zip Jakuhai Inexperienced / junior (kohai) tone Others — Machine-like, Kansai dialect, etc.

If you are unsure where to start, 若輩 (Jakuhai) is a good default.

docs.title: Step 2: Install the Voice into CoeiroInk
docs.text:
1. Extract the ZIP file — inside you will find a folder with an alphanumeric name (e.g. a1b2c3d4...).

  2. Copy that alphanumeric folder into the speaker_info folder inside your CoeiroInk installation directory:

    [CoeiroInk folder]\speaker_info\[alphanumeric folder]

  3. Launch (or restart) CoeiroInk.

  4. Click the character icon at the top of CoeiroInk to open the character dropdown — the new voice should now appear.

docs.title: Step 3: Register the Voice in YMM4
docs.text:
1. In YMM4, go to File → Edit character.
  2. Click the + button at the upper left to create a new character.
  3. Enter a Name (e.g. Kurosato Uzuki).
  4. Set Group to COEIROINK.
  5. Under Voice, click the ↻ (circular arrow icon) next to the voice dropdown.
  6. Select Reload COEIROINK v2 voices — this refreshes the available voice list.
  7. In the Voice dropdown, select COEIROINK2 / 白痴ー.
  8. The Style dropdown will be set automatically if only one style is installed (e.g. 若輩 / Jakuhai). If you have multiple styles installed, select the desired one manually.
  9. Adjust other settings as needed (volume, pitch, speed, intonation, etc.).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Each style variation is a separate download — you can install multiple variations of the same character.
  • If the voice still does not appear after reloading, restart YMM4 and try again.

docs.title: Terms of Use (白痴ー / Hakuchi)
docs.text:
• Commercial and non-commercial use: allowed.
  • Use in ads (games, manga apps, etc.): not allowed.
  • Modifications that closely resemble other existing characters: not allowed.
  • Must comply with CoeiroInk's own terms of use.

docs.title: Step 2: Download the FLUX Model
docs.text:

    • FLUX.1-dev — most popular, higher quality
    • FLUX.1-schnell — lighter and faster

  2. Place the .safetensors file in:

ComfyUI\models\checkpoints\

docs.title: Step 3: Install Required Nodes
docs.text:
FLUX is not standard Stable Diffusion and requires additional custom nodes.

  1. Open ComfyUI Manager.
  2. Click Install Custom Nodes.

  3. Search for and install:

    • Flux nodes
    • T5 loader
    • Updated sampler nodes (if prompted)

  4. Restart ComfyUI after installing.

docs.title: Step 4: Set Up the FLUX Workflow
docs.text:
Build the following node graph in ComfyUI:

Load Checkpoint (Flux)
       ↓
CLIP / T5 Text Encode
       ↓
KSampler
       ↓
VAE Decode
       ↓
Save Image

Note: FLUX uses a T5 text encoder instead of the classic CLIP encoder used in standard Stable Diffusion workflows.

cinematic portrait of a cyberpunk samurai, neon lighting, ultra detailed, 35mm photography

Setting Value Resolution 1024 × 1024 Steps 20–30 CFG scale 3–5

docs.title: Understand Spectrum in ComfyUI
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Spectrum is an inference acceleration technique for diffusion models. Instead of running the full UNet/DiT every step, it skips some steps by using predictions — achieving roughly 1.5–2× speed-up depending on settings.

docs.title: Recommended Nodes
docs.text:
Node Notes ComfyUI Spectrum SDXL Node (ruwwww) Best for general use — supports SDXL and Anima (DiT), easy to tune Spectrum SDXL Proper Closer to the paper; SDXL only; less customisable Anima-Enhancer Anima-specific; focused on image quality; not general-purpose

Start with ComfyUI Spectrum SDXL Node.

docs.title: window (most important)
docs.text:
• Small → stable but slower
  • Large → faster but prone to artifacts
  • Recommended starting value: 2–3

docs.title: Late-step behaviour
docs.text: Spectrum tends to produce artifacts in the final steps. Turn it off for the last 20% of steps to avoid this.

docs.title: Colour desaturation
docs.text: Prediction errors can reduce colour saturation. Enable the calibration feature or turn Spectrum off for the later steps.

docs.title: Recommended Starting Settings
docs.text: Setting Value window 2–3 m 2–3 lam 0.1–0.3 Last 20% of steps Spectrum off

docs.title: Run Google Security Checkup
docs.text: Use Google Security Checkup to review and improve the security of a Google account. The process verifies login activity, recovery settings, devices, and connected apps.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the Security Checkup page.

    https://myaccount.google.com/security-checkup

  2. Sign in with the Google account you want to review.

  3. Review Recent security activity.

    • Check for unknown login locations.
    • Check for unfamiliar devices.
    • If an activity is suspicious, select This wasn't me and follow the prompts.

  4. Verify Sign-in & recovery settings.

    • Confirm the password is secure.
    • Enable 2-Step Verification.

    To enable it:

    1. Open **2-Step Verification**.
2. Select a verification method:
    - SMS code
    - Authenticator app
    - Passkey

  5. Confirm Recovery information.

    • Verify the recovery email address.
    • Verify the recovery phone number.
    • Replace outdated contact information.

  6. Review Your devices.

    • Check the list of signed-in devices.
    • Select Sign out for devices that are not recognized.

  7. Review Third-party access.

    • Check apps connected through Sign in with Google.
    • Remove applications that are unused or untrusted.

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
Run Security Checkup periodically to maintain account security. Review settings again after:

  • Suspicious login alerts
  • Password changes
  • Installing new browser extensions
  • Connecting new apps to the account

docs.text: Change the access role of a user for a shared folder.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open Google Drive.
  2. Right-click the folder.
  3. Click Share.
  4. In the access list, locate the user.
  5. Click the role dropdown next to the user name.

  6. Select one of the following:

    • Viewer
    • Commenter
    • Editor

  7. Click Done.

docs.title: Role descriptions
docs.text:
• Viewer: Can view files only.
  • Commenter: Can view and add comments.
  • Editor: Can view, comment, edit, add, and delete files.

docs.title: Remove access
docs.text:
1. Open Share.
  2. Click the dropdown next to the user.

docs.title: Understand the Time & Pitch Module
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Time & Pitch module adjusts the speed and pitch of audio independently. It is primarily designed for musical material (instruments and vocals) rather than spoken voice, so options for speech processing are limited.

docs.title: Core Parameters
docs.text:
Stretch Ratio Controls playback speed. Lowering the value speeds up the audio; raising it slows it down.

Pitch Shift Controls pitch in semitones. Negative values lower the pitch; positive values raise it.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
Algorithm Best for Radius (best quality) Polyphonic material — instrument mixes, drum loops, rhythmic or non-harmonic audio Solo Instrument Monophonic material — solo strings, human voice Radius RT Polyphonic material where faster processing is needed; slightly lower quality than Radius

Note: Although Solo Instrument is described as suitable for human voice, Radius (best quality) often produces better results in practice. The optimal choice depends on the source material.

docs.title: Advanced Settings
docs.text: Setting Effect on Human Voice Transient sensitivity No noticeable effect Pitch coherence Minimal effect despite the description suggesting otherwise Adaptive window No noticeable effect Noise generation Setting to 0 reduces background noise — the most useful advanced setting for human voice

docs.title: Shift Formants
docs.text:
Formants are the resonance frequency components of a voice and are closely tied to characteristics such as gender and age. Enabling Shift Formants lets you adjust formants independently from pitch and time.

Setting Recommended value Notes Strength 1.0 (default) Higher values may increase perceived volume Shift [Semitones] Varies Negative values lower the voice character; this is the primary setting to adjust for human voice Width Default No noticeable effect on human voice

docs.title: Visualize Disk Usage on Windows
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Before backing up or cleaning up your system, it helps to see what's actually taking up space. This guide covers the best tool to visualize disk usage on Windows.

docs.title: Why Visualize First?
docs.text:
Blindly deleting files is risky. Visualizing disk usage lets you:

  • Instantly identify the largest files and folders
  • Make informed decisions about what to delete
  • Reduce backup size and time before copying to NAS or external storage

docs.title: WizTree (Windows)
docs.text:
⚡ Recommended — the fastest disk analyzer available for Windows.

WizTree reads directly from NTFS's MFT (Master File Table), bypassing the normal file system layer. This lets it scan even multi-terabyte drives in seconds.

docs.title: Download
docs.text: Item Details Official site https://www.diskanalyzer.com/ License Free for personal use Platform Windows 7 / 8 / 10 / 11

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Download and install WizTree from the official site.
  2. Launch WizTree and select the drive you want to scan (e.g. D:).
  3. Click Scan.
  4. The treemap view renders immediately — large rectangles = large files.
  5. Click any rectangle to reveal the full file path.
  6. Sort the file list by Size to find the top offenders.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Right-click any file in the list → Open Containing Folder to locate it quickly.
  • Use the Files tab (not just the treemap) to sort all files by size across the entire drive.
  • Filter by extension (e.g. .iso, .vhdx, .bak) to find specific file types.

Note: Always double-check before deleting. Some large files (e.g. page files, hibernation files) are system-managed and should not be removed manually.

docs.title: Suggested Workflow
docs.text:
# Step-by-step cleanup workflow

1. Scan D: with WizTree
2. Sort by Size (largest first)
3. Identify candidates for deletion:
   - Old installer files (.exe, .msi, .iso)
   - Unused virtual machine images (.vhdx, .vmdk)
   - Redundant backups or archives (.zip, .tar, .bak)
4. Delete or move to cold storage
5. Re-scan to confirm free space

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Once you've cleaned up Windows, consider also checking:

  • WSL disk usage — WSL2 virtual disk files (ext4.vhdx) can grow very large and do not shrink automatically even after deleting files inside Linux.
  • NAS / backup size — re-scan after cleanup to confirm how much you've saved before starting your backup job.

docs.title: Apply Nano Banana Prompting Best Practices
Apply Nano Banana Prompting Best Practices
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Official reference: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/ultimate-prompting-guide-for-nano-banana

Nano Banana models apply deep reasoning to fully understand your prompt before generating an image. Built on the Gemini 3 family, they support real-time web search, multimodal inputs, multilingual text rendering, and studio-quality visual controls.

docs.title: Core Best Practices
docs.text: Principle Description Be Specific Provide concrete details on subject, lighting, and composition Positive Framing Say "empty street" not "no cars" — describe what you want Control the Camera Use cinematic terms: "low angle," "aerial view," "f/1.8" Iterate Refine with follow-up prompts conversationally

docs.title: 01 — Image Generation
docs.text: Your prompt structure depends on whether you are using reference images or relying solely on text. You are the director — a simple list of keywords won't cut it.

docs.title: Text-to-Image (No References)
docs.text:
Starting from a blank canvas, describe the scene narratively.

Formula:

[Subject] + [Action] + [Location/Context] + [Composition] + [Style]

Example prompt:

A striking fashion model wearing a tailored brown dress, sleek boots, and holding a structured handbag. Posing with a confident, statuesque stance, slightly turned. A seamless, deep cherry red studio backdrop. Medium-full shot, center-framed. Fashion magazine style editorial, shot on medium-format analog film, pronounced grain, high saturation, cinematic lighting effect.

docs.title: Multimodal Generation (With References)
docs.text:
Combine up to 14 reference images in a single prompt — perfect for maintaining character consistency or merging a product into a new environment.

Formula:

[Reference Images] + [Relationship Instruction] + [New Scenario]

Example prompt:

Using the attached napkin sketch as the structure and the attached fabric sample as the texture, transform this into a high-fidelity 3D armchair render. Place it in a sun-drenched, minimalist living room.

docs.title: 02 — Image Editing
docs.text: Editing requires a different mindset. You already have a base image — focus your prompt on what is changing and, critically, what is staying the same.

docs.title: Conversational Editing (No New References)
docs.text:
Generate an image, then tweak it through natural conversation. Semantic masking lets you define a "mask" through text to edit only a specific part of an image.

  • Be explicit about what to keep exactly the same
  • Use clear, direct language for what to remove or change

Example prompt:

"Remove the man from the photo"

docs.title: Composition and Style Transfer (With New References)
docs.text:
Bring new images into the prompt to alter an existing one:

  • Adding elements: Upload a base image + an object image, then tell the model to combine them
  • Style transfer: Upload a photo and ask the model to recreate its content in a different artistic style (e.g., transform a city street into a Van Gogh painting)

docs.title: 03 — Real-Time Information from Web Search
docs.text:
Instead of describing a fictional scene, instruct the model to retrieve real-world data and then specify how to visualize it. Nano Banana 2 is powered by live web search.

Formula:

[Source/Search Request] + [Analytical Task] + [Visual Translation]

Example prompt:

Search for the current weather and date in San Francisco. Analytically, use this data to modify the scene (e.g., if raining, make it look grey and rainy). Visualize this in a miniature city-in-a-cup concept embedded within a realistic, modern smartphone UI.

docs.title: 04 — Text Rendering and Localization
docs.text:
Nano Banana excels at rendering sharp, legible text for posters, diagrams, and product mockups. It supports multilingual text generation in over 10 languages.

Key rules:

  • Enclose desired words in quotes — e.g., "Happy Birthday" or "URBAN EXPLORER"
  • Describe typography style or font name — e.g., "bold, white, sans-serif" or "Century Gothic 12px"
  • Write in one language, specify a different target language for output to localize
  • Text-first hack: First converse with the model to generate text concepts, then ask for an image with that text

Example prompt:

A high-end, glossy commercial beauty shot of a sleek, minimalist nude-colored face moisturizer jar on a warm studio background. Soft, radiant lighting. Render three lines of text: "GLOW" in a flowing Brush Script font; "10% OFF" in a heavy Impact font; "Your First Order" in a thin Century Gothic font. Then translate the text into Korean and Arabic.

docs.title: 05 — Prompting Like a Creative Director
docs.text: Stop typing keywords and start directing the scene. Elevate results from good to breathtaking with four studio-quality controls.

docs.title: Lighting
docs.text:
Tell the model exactly how the scene is illuminated.

Style Example Studio "Three-point softbox setup" Dramatic "Chiaroscuro lighting, harsh high contrast" Natural "Golden hour backlighting, long shadows"

docs.title: Camera, Lens and Focus
docs.text:
Dictate the exact camera type to change the visual DNA of the image.

Camera Effect GoPro Immersive, distorted action feel Fujifilm Authentic color science Disposable Raw, nostalgic flash aesthetic

For lenses: "f/1.8 shallow depth of field" / "wide-angle lens" / "macro lens"

docs.title: Color Grading and Film Stock
docs.text:
The texture and color of the image set the emotional tone.

  • Nostalgic/gritty: "1980s color film, slightly grainy"
  • Modern/moody: "Cinematic color grading, muted teal tones"

docs.title: Materiality and Texture
docs.text:
Define the physical makeup of every element — don't just name it, describe it.

Instead of... Say... "suit jacket" "navy blue tweed jacket" "armor" "ornate elven armor, etched with silver leaf patterns" "coffee mug" "minimalist ceramic coffee mug"

Warning: This is sync, not true backup. Deleting files on your phone may also delete them on the NAS. Enable versioning on your NAS to protect against accidental deletion.

docs.title: Step 1: Prepare Your NAS
docs.text:
1. Log in to DSM.
  2. Open Synology Drive Admin Console.
  3. Enable Team Folder if needed.
  4. Enable versioning (recommended: 10–20 versions).

docs.text:

  2. Tap More.
  3. Tap Backup and Sync Tasks.

docs.title: Local Path (Phone)
docs.text:
Choose the folder you want to back up. Examples:

Documents/
Download/

docs.title: Remote Path (NAS)
docs.text:
Choose or create a folder on your NAS. Example:

/home/Drive/PhoneBackup/Documents/

docs.title: Sync Mode
docs.text: Select Upload only. Files go from phone to NAS. Changes on the NAS do not affect your phone.

docs.title: Step 4: Adjust Sync Rules
docs.text:
• Enable syncing over Wi-Fi only (recommended).
  • Optionally restrict to charging state only.
  • Review file size limits if applicable.

docs.title: Step 5: Start the Sync
docs.text:
1. Confirm your settings.
  2. Tap Done / Apply.

Your files will now begin syncing.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Action on Phone Result on NAS Add file Uploaded Edit file Updated Delete file Deleted (see warning above)

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No true backup isolation — this is sync
  • Android limits full automation for arbitrary folders
  • No full device backup capability

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep documents in a dedicated folder (e.g., Documents/) for predictable sync behaviour.
  • Use a dedicated NAS folder (e.g., /home/Drive/PhoneBackup/) to avoid mixing with other files.
  • Enable versioning to protect against accidental deletion and file corruption.
  • Avoid editing the same files from multiple devices simultaneously.

This guide shows how to run Claude-powered workflows on a Synology NAS using Docker and the Anthropic API.

docs.title: 📌 Overview
docs.text:
Since Claude Desktop cannot run on Synology, the best approach is:

  • Run a lightweight app in Docker
  • Connect it to Claude via the Anthropic API
  • Use it for automation, chat interfaces, or file processing

docs.title: 📁 Step 3: Prepare a Project Folder

/docker/claude-app/

Inside it, create three files:

app.py
requirements.txt
Dockerfile

docs.title: app.py
docs.text:
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import requests
import os

app = Flask(__name__)

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")

@app.route("/chat", methods=["POST"])
def chat():
    user_input = request.json.get("message")

    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages",
        headers={
            "x-api-key": ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
            "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01",
            "content-type": "application/json"
        },
        json={
            "model": "claude-sonnet-4-6",
            "max_tokens": 500,
            "messages": [
                {"role": "user", "content": user_input}
            ]
        }
    )

    return jsonify(response.json())

@app.route("/")
def home():
    return "Claude API is running!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)

flask
requests

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY app.py .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

docs.text:
SSH into your Synology and run:

cd /volume1/docker/claude-app
docker build -t claude-app .

docs.title: ▶️ Step 6: Run the Container
docs.text:
docker run -d \
  -p 5000:5000 \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<YOUR-API-KEY> \
  --name claude-container \
  claude-app

docs.text:
Use curl to send a test message:

curl -X POST http://192.168.x.x:5000/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message": "Hello Claude"}'

You should receive a JSON response from Claude.

docs.text:

docs.title: Set Up Active Backup for Business for D: Drive Backup
Set Up Active Backup for Business for D: Drive Backup
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Active Backup for Business (ABB) is Synology's enterprise-grade agent-based backup solution. It enables you to back up your entire Windows PC — or selected volumes — directly to your NAS, with incremental transfers, global deduplication, and flexible restore options.

This guide covers:

  • Installing and configuring ABB on your NAS
  • Installing the agent on your Windows 11 machine
  • Creating a backup task targeting D:\ only
  • Setting schedule, deduplication, and retention
  • Configuring folder exclusions to save NAS space

Note: Your final setup will be professional-grade — Synology Drive handles real-time Obsidian vault sync, while ABB covers full D:\ drive backup and recovery.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Active Backup for Business on the NAS
docs.text:
1. Log into DSM (your NAS web interface).
  2. Open Package Center.
  3. Search for Active Backup for Business and click Install.
  4. Wait for installation to complete.

docs.title: Step 2: Open ABB and Enable PC Backup
docs.text:
1. Open Active Backup for Business from the DSM app menu.
  2. Navigate to the PC section in the left sidebar.
  3. Click Add Device — this will prompt you to download the Windows agent.

Note: Keep this browser window open — you will return to it after installing the agent on your PC.

docs.title: Step 3: Install the ABB Agent on Windows 11
docs.text:
1. Download the Active Backup for Business Agent installer from the ABB interface or from Synology's download center.
  2. Run the installer on your Windows 11 machine.
  3. Accept defaults and complete the installation.
  4. Launch the agent — it will open in the system tray.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect Your PC to the NAS
docs.text:
In the agent application on your Windows PC:

  1. Enter your NAS IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.x).
  2. Enter your DSM username and password.
  3. Click Connect.

Note: Your PC will now appear as a device in Active Backup for Business on the NAS. Return to the NAS browser tab to continue.

docs.title: Step 5: Create a Backup Task
docs.text:
In the ABB interface on your NAS:

  1. Select your PC from the device list.
  2. Click Create Task.

docs.title: Step 6: Select Customized Volume
docs.text:
When prompted to choose what to back up, you will see these options:

  • Entire device
  • System volume
  • Customized volume

Select Customized Volume, then tick D: drive only.

Note: This option backs up only D:\, avoiding wasted space on the C: system drive.

docs.title: Step 7: Set the Backup Schedule
docs.text: Option Description Recommended Daily — scheduled at night (e.g. 2:00 AM) while your PC is on Advanced Event-based: on startup, shutdown, or USB connect

docs.title: Step 8: Enable Deduplication and Compression
docs.text:
Both options are typically enabled by default. Verify they are on:

  • Global deduplication — eliminates duplicate data blocks across backups, saving significant NAS space
  • Compression — reduces backup size further

Note: Leave both enabled. These are among the most valuable features of ABB and cost little in performance.

docs.title: Step 9: Configure the Retention Policy
docs.text:
The retention policy determines how many recovery points are kept before old ones are deleted. It protects against accidental deletions and file corruption.

Recommended options:

  • Keep last 30 versions — simple and predictable
  • Smart Recycle — intelligent thinning that keeps more recent versions and gradually reduces older ones

Note: Smart Recycle is generally the best choice. It maximises recovery options while automatically managing space over time.

docs.title: Step 10: Apply and Run the First Backup
docs.text:
1. Review all settings and click Apply.
  2. The first backup will begin immediately (or at the next scheduled time).

Warning: The first backup will take a long time — it must scan and transfer the entire D:\ drive. All subsequent backups will be incremental (only changed data), which are much faster.

docs.title: Part 3: Folder Exclusions
docs.text: ABB supports file and folder exclusions to reduce backup size. Exclusions are applied as filters — not precise file selection — but they are effective for removing large, unimportant data.

docs.title: How to Access Exclusion Settings
docs.text:
1. Go to Active Backup for Business on your NAS.
  2. Select your PC backup task.
  3. Click Edit.
  4. Look for File Filter or Exclusion Settings.

docs.title: What You Can Exclude
docs.text:
By folder path — exclude entire folders using their full path:

D:\Games\
D:\Downloads\
D:\Temp\

By file type — exclude files by extension across the entire drive:

  • *.iso — disc images
  • *.tmp — temporary files
  • *.log — log files

docs.title: Recommended Exclusions
docs.text: Folder / Pattern Reason D:\Games\ Large game installs — easily re-downloadable D:\Downloads\ Ephemeral files with no long-term value D:\Temp\ Temporary files — not worth backing up *.iso Disc images — very large, easily re-sourced *.tmp Temporary files generated by apps *.log Log files — verbose, low value

docs.title: Exclusion Limitations
docs.text:
• ABB is fundamentally image-based — exclusions are filters, not precise file selection.
  • Path syntax must be exact — a typo means the folder is still backed up.
  • No auto-suggestions — you must know the exact paths.
  • Some system data may still be included even with exclusions.

Note: If your goal is to back up only a few specific folders (not exclude a few), use Synology Drive instead. ABB is best suited for "back up everything except X" scenarios.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
• Keep the NAS powered on during scheduled backup windows.
  • Verify sufficient free storage space on the NAS before the first run.
  • Use a wired LAN connection for the initial backup — significantly faster than Wi-Fi.
  • Enable Smart Recycle for automatic retention management.
  • Test a restore of a single file after setup to confirm everything works.

docs.title: Avoid This
docs.text:
• Do not run multiple backup tools on the same folder — this wastes space and causes conflicts.
  • Do not skip retention settings — unlimited versions will eventually fill your NAS.
  • Do not interrupt the first backup once started — let it complete fully.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tool Coverage and Purpose Synology Drive Obsidian Vault — real-time, versioned sync Active Backup for Business Entire D:\ drive — full incremental backup with restore

Use Synology NAS as a Claude Workflow Hub
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This guide documents the complete workflow for using Synology NAS as a central file hub between Windows PC (Claude Code) and Google Pixel (Claude mobile app). The setup uses only official tools — no third-party MCP connectors required.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Windows PC (<YOUR-PC>)
└── Claude Code
    └── <YOUR-FOLDER>\          ← local working folder
                │
                │  Synology Drive (Two-way sync)
                ▼
Synology DS720 NAS
└── <NAS-FOLDER>\               ← NAS mirror
                │
                │  Synology Drive app (read/write)
                ▼
Google Pixel
└── Claude app
    └── + button → upload file from Synology Drive app

docs.title: On Windows PC
docs.text:
1. Use Claude Code to create and edit files in your local working folder.
  2. Synology Drive automatically syncs all changes to the NAS in the background.
  3. No manual steps needed — files are always up to date on NAS.

docs.title: On Google Pixel
docs.text:
1. Open the Claude app.
  2. Tap the + button at the bottom of the chat window.
  3. Select the file from the Synology Drive app (e.g. a prompt or MD file created on PC).
  4. Ask Claude to generate a video script, SRT file, or any other output.
  5. Save the output back to NAS via the Synology Drive app if needed.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
Tool Platform Purpose Official Claude Code Windows PC File creation and editing ✅ Anthropic Synology Drive Client Windows PC Auto-sync local folder to NAS ✅ Synology Synology Drive app Google Pixel Access NAS files on mobile ✅ Synology Claude app Google Pixel AI generation using uploaded files ✅ Anthropic

Success

This workflow uses only official tools from Anthropic and Synology. No third-party MCP connectors are required.

docs.title: Why No MCP Connector?
docs.text:
During setup, a community-built MCP server (mcp-server-synology) was considered to allow Claude on Pixel to autonomously access NAS files. It was decided not to use it because:

  • It is not an official tool from Synology or Anthropic.
  • It requires storing NAS credentials in a config file.
  • The simpler alternative — uploading files via the + button in Claude app — achieves the same result safely.

When an official MCP connector becomes available from Synology or Anthropic, this workflow can be upgraded at that point.

Change Clothing in Anime Character Pack (Legacy)
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide explains how to swap the torso clothing on the male anime character in the Anime Character Pack (Legacy) by Studio SyndiCat. The pack uses a Construction Script inside the character Blueprint to apply meshes — so the correct method is through Class Defaults, not by editing mesh components directly.

docs.title: Available Tops for Male Characters
docs.text:
The pack includes three top options, located at: Content > AnimeCharacters > Blueprints > Characters > Male_Average > Tops

Folder Mesh Name Description Starter_TShirt skl_AnimeM_Top_Tshirt Red t-shirt Starter_Tank skl_AnimeM_Top_tank Black tank top Starter_Nak skl_AnimeM_Top_nak No top (naked body mesh)

docs.title: Why Not Edit the Component Directly?
docs.text:
The Blueprint's Construction Script sets the character's mesh components programmatically at runtime using variables from the Appearance category. If you change the Skeletal Mesh on the Top component directly — either in the Blueprint editor or as a level instance override — the Construction Script will override it back to the variable value. You must change the variable, not the component.

The screenshots below show what happens when you try the direct approach — the change does not stick.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Character Blueprint
docs.text: In the Outliner, find bp_AnimeCharacter and click the Edit bp_AnimeCharacter link next to it to open the Blueprint editor.

docs.title: Step 2: Open Class Defaults and Find the Appearance Section
docs.text:
In the Blueprint editor toolbar, click Class Defaults. In the Details panel on the right, scroll down to find the Appearance section. You will see four mesh variables:

  • Head Mesh
  • Torso Mesh
  • Bottom Mesh
  • Hair Mesh

docs.title: Step 3: Change the Torso Mesh
docs.text: Click the dropdown next to Torso Mesh (currently skl_AnimeM_Top_nak) and select the clothing mesh you want — for example, skl_AnimeM_Top_Tshirt for the red t-shirt.

docs.title: Step 4: Compile and Save
docs.text: Click Compile then Save in the Blueprint editor toolbar.

docs.title: Step 5: Return to the Main Viewport
docs.text: Close the Blueprint editor. The character in the viewport will now be wearing the selected top.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• This change applies to all instances of bp_AnimeCharacter in the level, because it modifies the Blueprint's class defaults.
  • The same Appearance section contains Bottom Mesh and Hair Mesh — use the same method to change pants or hairstyle.

• Slow generation
  • Occasional mispronunciation
  • High-end GPU recommended for comfort
  • Risk of misuse for voice deepfakes

docs.title: Recolor Hair Using Shader Color
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This method lets you change the overall hair color while keeping the highlight patterns in the texture intact.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the Material Texture Editor for the hair part you want to recolor (see Edit Hair Texture).
  2. In the left panel, scroll down to Color Calibration.
  3. Expand Shader Color.
  4. Check the Base Color checkbox and click its color swatch to choose your desired hair color.
  5. Optionally, also check Shade Color to control the shadow/shading tone separately.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Shader Color → Base Color applies the color at the rendering level, so the painted texture patterns (highlight blobs, hair flow details) are preserved.
  • This is different from Color Calibration → Main Color, which tints on top of the existing texture color — causing unwanted color blending (e.g. brown over purple → reddish).
  • For simple recoloring, Shader Color is the recommended approach. Use an external image editor only if you need fine-grained control over the texture itself.

  2. Open the Customize tab.

docs.title: Import Voice Lines via Scenario File in YMM4
Import Voice Lines via Scenario File in YMM4
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

YukkuriMovieMaker4 (YMM4) supports bulk voice generation by importing a scenario file (CSV or TXT). This lets you write all your dialogue in a spreadsheet and import it in one go, instead of typing lines one by one.

docs.title: CSV Format
docs.text:
The scenario file uses a simple two-column structure:

CharacterName,Dialogue text here
CharacterName,Another line of dialogue
Column Content A Character name (must exactly match the name registered in YMM4) B Dialogue / セリフ

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Yukkuri Reimu,Hello! Welcome to my channel.
YukkuriMarisa,Hey everyone, good to see you!
Yukkuri Reimu,Today we are going to talk about something interesting.
YukkuriMarisa,That sounds exciting! Let's get started.

Warning: The name in Column A must be identical to the registered character name in YMM4, including spaces (or lack thereof). For example: Yukkuri Reimu (with space) vs YukkuriMarisa (no space).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the CSV in Excel
docs.text:
1. Open Excel and enter character names in Column A, dialogue in Column B
  2. No headers — start data from row 1
  3. Save as: File → Save As → CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited)

Note: Save your scenario files to a dedicated folder, e.g. D:\02-assistant\projects\creator\ymm

docs.title: Step 2: Import into YMM4
docs.text:
1. In YMM4, go to File → Open scenario file
  2. Navigate to your CSV file and select it
  3. If a character name is unrecognized, a dropdown will appear — assign the correct character manually
  4. Review the lines in the scenario editor
  5. Click Add to timeline to generate all voice items at once

docs.title: Result
docs.text: YMM4 will automatically generate voice clips and place them sequentially on the timeline. Each line becomes its own voice item assigned to the correct character.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Supports .csv and .txt formats (shown in file dialog as Scenario file (*.csv;*.txt))
  • Long lines may affect timing — keep dialogue concise per line
  • Voice speed, pitch, and other settings are applied from each character's existing YMM4 configuration
  • Scenario files can be edited and re-imported to regenerate voice lines in bulk

docs.title: Migrate Claude Code from npm to Native Installer
Migrate Claude Code from npm to Native Installer
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text:
When launching Claude Code in VS Code (WSL/Ubuntu), the following message appears in the terminal:

Claude Code has switched from npm to native installer.
Run `claude install` or see https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/getting-started
X Auto-update failed · Try `claude doctor` or `npm i -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`

docs.title: Cause
docs.text: Anthropic released a native binary installer for Claude Code in October 2025, replacing the previous npm-based installation. The old npm version detects this and prompts you to migrate. The native installer is simpler, more stable, and does not require Node.js.

docs.title: Step 1: Run the Migration Command
docs.text:
In your terminal (any directory is fine):

claude install

Expected output:

✓ Claude Code successfully installed!

  Version: 2.1.x
  Location: ~/.local/bin/claude

  Next: Run `claude --help` to get started

⚠ Setup notes:
  • Native installation exists but ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH. Run:

  echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Step 2: Add ~/.local/bin to Your PATH
docs.text:
If the setup notes warn that ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, run:

echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Step 3: Verify the Installation
docs.text:
which claude

Expected output:

/home/<username>/.local/bin/claude

If this is correct, the migration is complete.

docs.title: Step 4: Restart VS Code
docs.text: Restart VS Code to ensure all terminals and extensions pick up the new PATH. The warning message should no longer appear.

docs.title: which claude Still Points to an asdf or nvm Shim
docs.text:
If you use a Node.js version manager like asdf or nvm, its shim may still take priority. Uninstall the old npm package from your Node.js versions:

# For asdf
for version in $(asdf list nodejs | tr -d ' *'); do
  echo "Uninstalling from nodejs $version..."
  ASDF_NODEJS_VERSION=$version npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code 2>/dev/null
done

# For nvm
nvm use <version> && npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Then confirm again:

which claude
# Should now show: /home/<username>/.local/bin/claude

docs.title: General Health Check
docs.text:
claude doctor

This command reports any issues with your installation, such as missing binaries or PATH problems.

docs.title: Set Up Claude Code in WSL2
Set Up Claude Code in WSL2
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Set up Claude Code in a WSL2 Ubuntu environment and connect it to an existing MkDocs project.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• WSL2 running Ubuntu
  • VS Code with the Remote – WSL extension installed
  • An existing MkDocs project with a Python venv

docs.title: Step 1: Set Up the Folder Structure
docs.text:
Create a dedicated folder for your Claude Code projects:

mkdir -p ~/projects/02-assistant/python/mkdocs

The suggested structure is:

~/projects/
└── 02-assistant/
    └── python/
        └── mkdocs/       ← Claude Code project root

docs.title: Step 2: Install Node.js
docs.text:
Claude Code requires Node.js 18 or later. Install it via nvm (Node Version Manager):

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash

Restart your terminal, then install and activate Node.js:

nvm install --lts
nvm use --lts

Verify the installation:

node --version

docs.title: Step 3: Install Claude Code
docs.text:
Install Claude Code globally via npm:

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Verify the installation:

claude --version

docs.title: Step 4: First Launch and Authentication
docs.text:
Navigate to your project folder and launch Claude Code:

cd ~/projects/02-assistant/python/mkdocs
claude

On first launch, Claude Code will prompt you to authenticate:

  1. A browser window opens at claude.ai.
  2. Log in with your Anthropic account.
  3. Copy the authorisation code displayed in the browser.
  4. Paste it back into the terminal prompt.

Claude Code stores the session token locally. You will not need to re-authenticate on subsequent launches.

docs.title: Step 5: Choose How to Use Claude Code
docs.text: There are two ways to run Claude Code depending on your workflow:

docs.title: Option A: VS Code Terminal (Recommended for development)
docs.text:
1. Open VS Code.
  2. Connect to WSL2 via the Remote – WSL extension (F1 → Remote-WSL: New Window).
  3. Open your project folder in VS Code.
  4. Open the integrated terminal (Ctrl+`).
  5. Run claude from the terminal.

Claude Code runs in the same shell as your project, with full access to the filesystem and git history.

docs.title: Option B: Claude Desktop (Recommended for general tasks)
docs.text:
1. Install Claude Desktop on Windows.
  2. Open Claude Desktop and sign in.
  3. Use the built-in Claude Code integration to connect to your WSL2 filesystem.

Use Option B when you want a graphical interface without opening VS Code.

docs.title: Step 6: Recreate the venv After Copying a Project
docs.text:
If you copied or moved the project folder, the existing .venv will have broken absolute paths. Delete it and rebuild:

cd ~/projects/02-assistant/python/mkdocs
rm -rf .venv

Install python3-venv if it is not already available:

sudo apt install python3-venv

Create a fresh virtual environment and install dependencies:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

(.venv) will appear at the start of your terminal prompt when the environment is active.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify with MkDocs Serve
docs.text:
With the venv active, start the local development server:

mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser. If the site loads correctly, the setup is complete.

To stop the server, press Ctrl+C.

terminal

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Open Docker Desktop.

  2. Go to Settings.

  3. Navigate to Resource → WSL integration.

    1. Enable:
      • Enable integration with my default WSL distro.
      • Ubuntu under Enable integration with additional distros.
    2. Click Apply & restart.

  4. Restart VS Code.

Install Python Packages with pip in Docker
docs.text: Install MkDocs and related plugins inside a Docker image using requirements.txt.

docs.title: What this guide does
docs.text:
• Explains how pip install works inside Docker
  • Shows the correct Dockerfile setup
  • Explains when you must rebuild the image
  • Prevents common dependency issues

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create or update requirements.txt.

    mkdocs<2
mkdocs-material
mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin
mkdocs-static-i18n
mkdocs-glightbox

    Add or remove packages as needed.

  2. Install dependencies during Docker build.

    In your Dockerfile, include:

    FROM python:3.12-slim

RUN apt-get update \
&& apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git \
&& rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN git config --system --add safe.directory /mkdocs

WORKDIR /mkdocs

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["mkdocs", "serve", "-a", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

    Important:

    • COPY requirements.txt . happens before copying the whole project.
    • pip install runs during build, not during docker run.

  3. Build the image.

    docker build -t my-mkdocs .

    If you changed requirements.txt, use:

    docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .

  4. Run the container.

    docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

docs.title: pip install does NOT run during docker run
docs.text:
This command:

docker run ...

does not install packages.

All Python dependencies must already be installed during:

docker build

docs.title: When you must rebuild
docs.text:
Rebuild if you change:

  • requirements.txt
  • Dockerfile
  • Python version in FROM python:...

You do not need to rebuild for:

  • Markdown changes
  • CSS changes
  • HTML override changes
  • mkdocs.yml changes

docs.title: Optional: Verify installed packages
docs.text:
Run:

docker run --rm -it my-mkdocs pip list

Or check MkDocs version:

docker run --rm -it my-mkdocs mkdocs --version

docs.title: Why this pattern is recommended
docs.text:
This order:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

improves build caching.

Docker only re-installs dependencies when requirements.txt changes.

Content edits do not trigger re-installation.

This setup ensures:

  • Clean dependency management
  • Reproducible builds
  • Correct behavior in Docker + GitHub Actions
  • Stable MkDocs 1.x environment

docs.title: Prevent Zone.Identifier Files in Linux
docs.text: Zone.Identifier files can appear in repositories when Windows attaches security metadata to files downloaded from the internet. When working with Linux tools through WSL, Git, or Docker, these metadata streams may appear as real files and pollute the project directory.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Work inside the Linux filesystem instead of Windows-mounted paths.

    Store projects inside the WSL Linux home directory:

    ~/projects/my-repo

    Avoid storing repositories in Windows-mounted locations such as:

    /mnt/c/Users/<user>/projects

    Linux filesystems do not support Windows Alternate Data Streams, so Zone.Identifier files are not created.

  2. Clone repositories inside WSL.

    Run Git commands from the Linux shell:

    git clone https://github.com/example/repo.git

    Avoid cloning repositories through Windows Explorer or Windows Git clients.

  3. Download files using Linux tools.

    Download files from inside WSL using tools such as:

    curl -O https://example.com/file.tar.gz

    or

    wget https://example.com/file.tar.gz

    Files downloaded in Linux do not receive Windows security streams.

  4. Edit files using WSL-aware editors.

    Use editors that interact directly with the Linux filesystem:

    • Visual Studio Code with the Remote – WSL extension
    • vim
    • nano

    Avoid editing project files through Windows Explorer under \\wsl$.

  5. Extract archives inside Linux.

    Extract downloaded archives using Linux tools:

    tar -xzf archive.tar.gz

    Avoid extracting archives using Windows Explorer before moving them into the repository.

  6. Block metadata files in Git.

    Add rules to .gitignore:

    Thumbs.db
desktop.ini
*.Zone.Identifier

    This prevents accidental commits if the files appear.

  7. Remove existing Zone.Identifier files.

    If metadata files already exist in a repository, remove them:

    find . -name "*:Zone.Identifier" -delete

    Verify the working tree afterwards:

    git status

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Windows creates Zone.Identifier using the Mark of the Web security mechanism. When files are downloaded or copied from external sources in Windows environments, the metadata may appear as separate files when accessed from Linux tooling. Keeping repositories entirely inside the Linux filesystem prevents the issue.

docs.title: Deploy with gh-deploy
docs.text: mkdocs gh-deploy is a built-in MkDocs command that builds your site locally and pushes the generated files directly to the gh-pages branch. This method does not use GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Warning

Do not use mkdocs gh-deploy if your repository is configured to deploy using GitHub Actions. Choose one deployment method and use it consistently:

  • GitHub Actions > automated deployment on push
  • mkdocs gh-deploy > manual deployment from your local machine

Mixing both methods can cause confusion.

docs.title: When should you use gh-deploy?
docs.text:
Use this method if:

  • You do not want to use GitHub Actions
  • You prefer manual deployment
  • You want the simplest possible setup
  • You are working on a small personal project

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When you run:

mkdocs gh-deploy

MkDocs will:

  1. Build the site locally
  2. Create (or update) the gh-pages branch
  3. Push the built site to GitHub
  4. Publish it via GitHub Pages

docs.text:

docs.title: Display the Revision Date at the Bottom
Display the Revision Date at the Bottom
docs.text: Display the Git revision date in the default Material footer area using mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Add the plugin to requirements.txt.

    mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin

    Pin MkDocs to 1.x:

    mkdocs<2

  2. Enable the plugin in mkdocs.yml.

    plugins:
  - i18n:
      # your existing i18n configuration
  - git-revision-date-localized:
      type: date
      timezone: Asia/Tokyo
      custom_format: "%Y-%m-%d"
      fallback_to_build_date: true
  - search
  - glightbox

  3. Configure GitHub Actions to fetch full history.

    In .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    fetch-depth: 0

    Install dependencies:

    - run: pip install -r requirements.txt

  4. Install git in the Docker image.

    Update Dockerfile:

    FROM python:3.12-slim

RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /mkdocs
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["mkdocs", "serve", "-a", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

  5. Allow Git to read the mounted repository.

    Add after installing git:

    RUN git config --system --add safe.directory /mkdocs

  6. Rebuild and run.

    docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .
docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

  7. Verify the result.

    Open:

    • http://localhost:8000/kb/
    • http://localhost:8000/kb/ja/

    Confirm that the revision date appears in the bottom metadata area (clock icon section).

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
If the message “Unable to read git logs… Falling back to build date” appears:

  • Ensure .git exists in the mounted directory.
  • Confirm safe.directory /mkdocs is configured.
  • Confirm fetch-depth: 0 is set in GitHub Actions.

If a MkDocs 2.0 compatibility warning appears, verify:

mkdocs --version

Ensure the version is 1.x and mkdocs<2 is pinned in requirements.txt.

docs.title: Display the Revision Date at the Top
Display the Revision Date at the Top
docs.text: Display the Git revision date at the top of each page using Material for MkDocs. Hide the default footer date and exclude the home pages.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Enable theme overrides in mkdocs.yml.

    theme:
  name: material
  custom_dir: overrides

  2. Create the override file.

    Create:

    `overrides/main.html`

  3. Add the template logic.

    {% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}

  {% set is_home = page.file.src_path.endswith("index.md") %}

  {% if page.meta.git_revision_date_localized and not is_home %}
    <div class="page-date">
      {% if config.theme.language == "ja" %}
        最終更新日: {{ page.meta.git_revision_date_localized }}
      {% else %}
        Last updated: {{ page.meta.git_revision_date_localized }}
      {% endif %}
    </div>
  {% endif %}

  {{ super() }}

{% endblock %}

    This:

    • Displays the revision date above the page content.
    • Hides the date on en/index.md and ja/index.md.
    • Switches the label based on the active language.

  4. Create the stylesheet.

    Create:

    `docs/stylesheets/extra.css`

  5. Add the styling and hide the footer date.

    .page-date {
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  color: #888;
  margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
  font-weight: 400;
}

.md-source-file {
  display: none;
}

    This:

    • Styles the top date as metadata.
    • Removes the default footer revision block.

  6. Register the stylesheet in mkdocs.yml.

    extra_css:
  - stylesheets/extra.css

  7. Rebuild the Docker image.

    docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .
docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
Do not create overrides/partials/content.html with:

{% extends "partials/content.html" %}

This causes a recursion error because the override extends itself.

Verify:

  • The date appears at the top of normal pages.
  • The date does not appear on index.md.
  • The footer revision block is no longer displayed.

docs.title: Host a Private MkDocs Site on Synology NAS
Host a Private MkDocs Site on Synology NAS
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide shows how to serve a static MkDocs site from a Synology NAS on your local network using Web Station, so the site is always accessible without running mkdocs serve.

Requirements:

  • Synology NAS running DSM 7
  • MkDocs project in WSL2 on Windows 11
  • Admin access to DSM

docs.title: Step 1: Install Web Station
docs.text:
1. Open Package Center on the NAS.
  2. Search for Web Station.
  3. Click Install.

After installation, Web Station automatically creates a Default Portal on port 80. No new portal needs to be created.

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Shared Folder Permissions
docs.text:
1. Open Control Panel → Shared Folder.
  2. Select web → Edit → Permissions.
  3. Confirm your user account has Read/Write access.

docs.title: Step 3: Install cifs-utils in WSL2
docs.text: sudo apt-get install cifs-utils

docs.title: Step 4: Mount the NAS Web Folder in WSL2
docs.text:
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nas-web
sudo mount -t cifs //192.168.x.x/web /mnt/nas-web -o username=<YOUR-VALUE>,uid=1000,gid=1000

Replace 192.168.x.x with your NAS IP address. Enter your NAS password when prompted.

Note: To find your NAS IP, open Control Panel → Network → Network Interface tab.

Note: This mount does not persist after a reboot. Repeat this step each time you restart WSL2.

docs.title: Step 5: Build and Sync the Site
docs.text:
.venv/bin/mkdocs build
mkdir /mnt/nas-web/kb
rsync -av --delete site/ /mnt/nas-web/kb/

The mkdir line is only needed the first time.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify
docs.text: Open a browser and go to http://192.168.x.x/kb/. The site should load.

docs.title: Updating the Site
docs.text:
Each time you update content, run the following steps:

  1. Mount the NAS web folder (skip this step if WSL2 has not been restarted since the last sync):
sudo mount -t cifs //192.168.x.x/web /mnt/nas-web -o username=<YOUR-VALUE>,uid=1000,gid=1000
  1. Build the site:
.venv/bin/mkdocs build
  1. Sync the build output to the NAS:
rsync -av --delete site/ /mnt/nas-web/kb/

docs.title: Migrate MkDocs from Docker to venv
Migrate MkDocs from Docker to venv
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Move an existing MkDocs project from a Docker-based setup to a lightweight Python virtual environment (venv) on WSL2.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• WSL2 running Ubuntu
  • An existing MkDocs project set up with Docker
  • Git configured and connected to GitHub

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Files to Copy
docs.text:
From your Docker project folder, copy the following:

Item Description docs/ Markdown content overrides/ Custom theme overrides mkdocs.yml Site configuration requirements.txt Plugin and dependency list .git/ Git history .github/ GitHub Actions workflows

Leave these behind:

Item Reason Dockerfile Docker-specific, no longer needed site/ Generated output — MkDocs will rebuild it

docs.title: Step 2: Check for Unexpected Files
docs.text:
Run the following to inspect your project folder:

ls -la ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/

If you find an unrecognised file, check its contents before deleting:

cat ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/<filename>

To delete it:

rm ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/<filename>

docs.title: Step 3: Create the New Folder
docs.text: mkdir -p ~/projects/python/mkdocs

docs.title: Step 4: Copy Files with rsync
docs.text:
Use rsync to copy everything across, excluding Docker-specific files and the generated site/ folder:

rsync -av \
  --exclude='Dockerfile' \
  --exclude='site/' \
  ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/ \
  ~/projects/python/mkdocs/

docs.title: Step 5: Set Up the venv
docs.text:
Navigate to the new folder:

cd ~/projects/python/mkdocs

If python3-venv is not installed, install it first:

sudo apt install python3-venv

Create and activate the virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

(.venv) will appear at the start of your terminal prompt when the venv is active.

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Site Locally
docs.text:
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser to confirm the site looks correct.

docs.title: Step 7: Test the GitHub Workflow
docs.text:
Make a small edit to any file in docs/, then commit and push:

git add .
git commit -m "test: verify new venv setup"
git push

Check the Actions tab in your GitHub repository to confirm the deployment workflow completes successfully.

docs.title: Step 8: Remove the Old Docker Folder
docs.text:
Once everything is confirmed working, delete the old project folder:

rm -rf ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs

Warning: rm -rf is irreversible. Double-check the path before running.

docs.title: Publish a Docker-Based Site to GitHub Pages
Publish a Docker-Based Site to GitHub Pages
docs.text: This guide assumes you build and preview MkDocs inside Docker, and publish to GitHub Pages using GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A GitHub account
  • A MkDocs project folder that contains:
  • mkdocs.yml
  • docs/ (your Markdown pages)
  • Docker installed locally (for preview/build)
  • Git installed locally (for pushing to GitHub)

docs.title: 1) Create a GitHub repository
docs.text:
1. Log in to GitHub.

  2. Click New to create a repository.

  3. Set the following options:

    • Repository name: Any name
    • Description: Any description
    • Choose visibility: Public (required for free GitHub Pages on personal accounts)
    • Add README: Off (optional)
    • Add .gitignore: No (optional)
    • Add license: No (optional)

  4. The repository is created.

docs.title: 2) Preview the site locally
docs.text:
1. In the project root folder in VS Code, run:

    docker run --rm -it \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v "$(pwd)":/mkdocs \
  my-mkdocs \
  mkdocs serve -a 0.0.0.0:8000

    Tip

    Make sure your Docker image my-mkdocs is already built.

  2. Open the local site:

    http://localhost:8000

docs.title: 3) Initialize git and push the files to GitHub
docs.text:
1. In the project root folder in VS Code, run:

    git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial MkDocs site"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/REPO_NAME.git
git push -u origin main

    Note

    • If you already ran git init, skip it.

    • If origin already exists, update it:

      git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/REPO_NAME.git

docs.title: 4) Add a GitHub Actions workflow to build and deploy
docs.text:
1. Create the workflow folder in the project root:

    mkdir -p .github/workflows

  2. Create and open the workflow file:

    nano .github/workflows/deploy.yml

  3. Add the following content:

    name: Deploy MkDocs

on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: "pages"
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.x"

      # Install the same plugins used locally
      # Prefer: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - run: |
          pip install \
            mkdocs \
            mkdocs-material \
            mkdocs-static-i18n \
            mkdocs-glightbox

      - run: mkdocs build

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: site

      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

  4. Commit and push the workflow:

    git add .github/workflows/deploy.yml
git commit -m "Add GitHub Pages deployment workflow"
git push

  5. Open the Actions tab and confirm that the workflow completes successfully (green ✅).

docs.title: 5) Enable GitHub Pages (use GitHub Actions as the source)
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Pages.

  2. Under Build and deployment > Source, select GitHub Actions.

  3. The site should be available at:

    https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/REPO_NAME/

    Note

    Changes are published after the GitHub Actions workflow completes. If updates do not appear immediately, wait for the green ✅ in Actions and refresh the page.

docs.title: Publish a Site Using GitHub Pages
Publish a Site Using GitHub Pages
docs.text:
1. Connect your project to GitHub.

    terminal
    git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial MkDocs site"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/your-repo-name.git
git push -u origin main

  2. Deploy to GitHub Pages.

    terminal
    mkdocs gh-deploy

    Note

    This command:

    • Builds your site
    • Creates a gh-pages branch
    • Pushes the static HTML to that branch
    • GitHub Pages serves it automatically

  3. Enable GitHub Pages in your GitHub repository: Go to Settings → Pages, then set:

    • Source: Deploy from a branch
    • Branch: gh-pages / root

  4. Your site will be available at:

    https://yourusername.github.io/your-repo-name/

docs.title: Rebuild the MkDocs Docker Image Only When Needed
Rebuild the MkDocs Docker Image Only When Needed
docs.text: Use this guide to decide when you must run docker build before docker run for your MkDocs container.

docs.title: What this guide does
docs.text:
• Explains when a rebuild is required
  • Explains when a rebuild is not required (because you mount the repo with -v $(pwd):/mkdocs)
  • Provides a simple repeatable workflow

docs.title: When you must rebuild
docs.text:
Rebuild the image when you change something that affects what’s installed inside the image:

  • Dockerfile (example: adding git, safe.directory, changing CMD, changing base image)
  • requirements.txt (adding/removing/upgrading Python packages)
  • Anything else that is only applied during docker build (system packages installed with apt-get, etc.)

Run:

docker build -t my-mkdocs .

Use --no-cache only when you want to force a completely fresh build (useful after dependency changes or when you suspect caching issues):

docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .

docs.title: When you do not need to rebuild
docs.text:
Because you run with a bind mount:

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

You do not need to rebuild when you change files that are read directly from the mounted repo at runtime, such as:

  • Markdown content in docs/**
  • CSS in docs/stylesheets/** (example: extra.css)
  • Theme overrides in overrides/** (example: overrides/main.html)
  • mkdocs.yml (config changes are picked up when MkDocs reloads)

In these cases, do this instead:

  • Refresh the browser (hard refresh if needed)
  • If live reload does not pick it up, stop the container and run docker run ... again

docs.title: Recommended workflow for local editing
docs.text:
1. Start the container:

    docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

  2. Edit files (.md, .css, overrides/*.html, mkdocs.yml).

  3. If you changed Dockerfile or requirements.txt, rebuild and restart:

    docker build -t my-mkdocs .
docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

docs.title: Note
docs.text: If you ever remove the -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mount and rely only on COPY . . inside the image, then every content/CSS/HTML change will require a rebuild.

docs.title: Understand the Docker Run Command
docs.text:
This guide explains the meaning of the following Docker command and how image names like mkdocs-dev and my-mkdocs affect behavior.

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mkdocs-dev

docs.title: 1. Basic structure of docker run
docs.text:
General syntax:

docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE_NAME [COMMAND]

Example:

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mkdocs-dev

Components:

Part Meaning docker run Start a new container OPTIONS Configure container behavior IMAGE_NAME The environment to run COMMAND Optional override command

docs.title: --rm
docs.text:
--rm

Meaning:

  • Automatically deletes the container after it stops

Why useful:

  • Keeps system clean
  • Avoids unused container buildup

Without --rm:

Container remains after exit.

With --rm:

Container is deleted automatically.

docs.title: -it
docs.text:
-it

This is combination of:

-i   (interactive)
-t   (terminal)

Meaning:

  • Allows interactive use
  • Shows logs and output in your terminal
  • Lets you press Ctrl+C to stop

Required for development servers like MkDocs.

docs.title: -p 8000:8000
docs.text:
-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT

Example:

-p 8000:8000

Meaning:

  • Maps port from container → host machine

Structure:

host:container

Result:

Browser → localhost:8000 → Docker container port 8000

This allows you to open MkDocs in your browser:

http://localhost:8000

docs.title: -v $(pwd):/mkdocs
docs.text:
-v HOST_FOLDER:CONTAINER_FOLDER

Example:

-v $(pwd):/mkdocs

Meaning:

Mounts your current directory into the container.

Breakdown:

Part Meaning $(pwd) Your current folder on host /mkdocs Folder inside container

Result:

Your files → available inside container

Example:

Host:

/home/user/docs

Container:

/mkdocs

MkDocs reads files from /mkdocs.

Changes update instantly.

docs.title: 3. Image name
docs.text:
Final part of command:

mkdocs-dev

This is the Docker image name.

Docker images are like:

  • Templates
  • Environments
  • Preconfigured systems

They contain:

  • OS
  • Python
  • MkDocs
  • plugins
  • themes

docs.title: 4. Example: mkdocs-dev vs my-mkdocs
docs.text:
Two commands:

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mkdocs-dev

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

Difference:

Only the image name:

Image Meaning mkdocs-dev Image named mkdocs-dev my-mkdocs Image named my-mkdocs

They may contain different:

  • MkDocs version
  • plugins
  • themes
  • Python version

Example:

mkdocs-dev:

MkDocs only

my-mkdocs:

MkDocs + Material theme + plugins

docs.title: 5. Visual diagram
docs.text:
Your Computer

/docs folder
   │
   │ mounted via -v
   ▼
Docker Container

/mkdocs folder
   │
   │ served by MkDocs
   ▼
Port 8000 inside container
   │
   │ mapped via -p
   ▼
localhost:8000 on your computer

docs.title: 6. Real example workflow
docs.text:
Step 1: Build image

docker build -t my-mkdocs .

Step 2: Run server

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

Step 3: Open browser

http://localhost:8000

docs.title: 7. Summary table
docs.text: Part Meaning docker run Start container --rm Delete container after stop -it Interactive terminal -p 8000:8000 Map ports -v $(pwd):/mkdocs Mount folder mkdocs-dev / my-mkdocs Image name

docs.title: 8. Key concept summary
docs.text:
Docker image = Environment

Docker container = Running instance of image

Your command means:

"Run MkDocs inside Docker, use my current folder, and show it on localhost:8000"

docs.title: 9. Check available images
docs.text:
docker images

Example output:

REPOSITORY   TAG
mkdocs-dev   latest
my-mkdocs    latest

docs.title: 10. Stop container
docs.text:
Press:

Ctrl + C

Container is removed automatically because of --rm.

docs.title: Understand the MkDocs 2.0 Warning
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This warning is from the Material for MkDocs team, alerting you about the upcoming MkDocs 2.0 release. It's not an error — your setup is working fine — but it's a heads-up worth paying attention to.

docs.title: What's Happening
docs.text:
MkDocs 2.0 is a new major version of the underlying framework, but the Material for MkDocs team is warning that it's essentially incompatible with the current ecosystem:

  • The plugin system is being removed, so any plugins you use will break
  • The theming system is being rewritten, so Material's theme itself won't work
  • There's no migration path from MkDocs 1.x projects
  • It's currently unlicensed and has a closed contribution model

docs.title: What You Should Do (For Now): Nothing
docs.text: This is a warning about a future version, not something that's broken today. Your current Docker setup with Material for MkDocs is fine. The team is essentially signaling they won't be supporting MkDocs 2.0, and advising users not to upgrade when it releases.

docs.title: Longer Term
docs.text:
• Stay on MkDocs 1.x with Material for MkDocs for the foreseeable future
  • Watch the Material for MkDocs blog/repo — they may announce an alternative path or their own fork
  • Pin your MkDocs version in your Dockerfile or requirements.txt (e.g. mkdocs>=1.5,<2.0) to avoid accidentally pulling in 2.0

You can read the full analysis at the URL in the warning if you want the complete picture from the Material team's perspective.

docs.title: Understand MkDocs Packages
docs.text: Package Description mkdocs The core engine — turns Markdown into a website. mkdocs-material Theme: beautiful typography, dark mode, search, icons, diagrams (including Mermaid!), callouts, tabs, grids — the works. mkdocs-awesome-pages-plugin Lets you organize pages in folders without manually declaring everything in mkdocs.yml. mkdocs-glightbox Adds a sleek lightbox for images — perfect for documentation with screenshots or diagrams.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Page File
docs.text:
Create the new documentation page inside the docs/ directory:

docs/outlook.md

MkDocs automatically detects files in docs/, but they will not appear in navigation unless added to mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: Step 2: Add the Page to Navigation in mkdocs.yml
docs.text:
MkDocs only shows pages in the left navigation if they are included in the nav: section.

Example:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Outlook: outlook.md

If your site is bilingual, make sure to add the page in both language configs if applicable.

docs.title: Step 3: Commit and Push Both the New File and the Config Change
docs.text: Both the page file and the mkdocs.yml change must be committed and pushed. Otherwise, the page may exist but will not appear in navigation.

docs.title: Method 1: Commit Everything (Most Common)
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "Add Outlook page"
git push

docs.title: Method 2: Stage Only the Files You Changed
docs.text:
git add docs/outlook.md mkdocs.yml
git commit -m "Add Outlook page to nav"
git push

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The key point is:

mkdocs.yml must be committed and pushed for navigation changes to appear.

If you updated configuration such as navigation or language links, commit and push:

git add mkdocs.yml
git commit -m "Update navigation or fix language switch links"
git push

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
After pushing:

  • The new page will appear in the left navigation
  • The site will rebuild automatically
  • The updated configuration will be applied
  • GitHub Pages (or your deployment target) will publish the updated site

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
To update the site:

  1. Create the page file in docs/
  2. Add the page to nav: in mkdocs.yml
  3. Commit and push both the page and the config

Configuration changes do not take effect until they are committed and pushed.

docs.title: View Deployment Errors
docs.text: You can view deployment errors from the Actions tab in your repository.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Go to your repository on GitHub.

  2. Click the Actions tab, then select the workflow run that shows a failed status (❌).

  3. In the workflow details, click build-deploy.

  4. Review the logs to identify the error.

docs.title: Tip
docs.text:
• Expand individual steps to see detailed error messages.
  • The error message is usually shown in the step marked with a ❌ icon.
